description: Ubuntu Bare Bears presents THE LAST SIGNAL: ABANDONED, NOT FORGOTTEN, an immersive space adventure where players explore abandoned NASA equipment on the Moon and Mars, uncover scientific discoveries, solve challenges, and restore missing mission records to find their way home. It transforms space history into an interactive journey of curiosity, exploration, and discovery.
summary:
"The Last Signal: Abandoned, But Not Forgotten" is a browser-based space exploration game developed by Ubuntu Bare Bears. It takes players on an interactive journey from Earth to the Moon and Mars, introducing six NASA exploration systems: Apollo 11's Lunar Module Eagle, the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), Sojourner, Opportunity and InSight.

Through interactive exploration and storytelling, players discover what these machines were designed to do, how they operated, what they achieved and why their missions ended. Our project addresses NASA's discarded-equipment storytelling challenge by turning mission history into an engaging experience rather than simply presenting facts. We aim to make space science more accessible to young people, inspire curiosity about engineering and exploration, and highlight the lasting value of scientific discoveries. Even when a mission ends, the knowledge it leaves behind continues to inspire future exploration.
details:
The Last Signal is a first-person, browser-based 3D space exploration game that takes players on an adventure from Earth to the Moon and Mars. The experience is structured around six mission levels, each introducing players to real NASA exploration equipment and the stories behind it. The journey begins on Earth, where players encounter a mysterious glowing green object inside their refrigerator. After interacting with it, they are unexpectedly transported into space and find themselves stranded far from home. Their only way back to Earth is to explore the Moon and Mars, complete their missions, and learn about the equipment left behind on these worlds.

On the Moon, players meet Moona, a fictional guide who introduces them to lunar exploration equipment, including Apollo 11's Lunar Module Eagle, the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), and the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP). Players then continue to Mars, where they meet Mimi, another fictional guide who introduces them to Sojourner, Opportunity, and InSight. Throughout the six mission levels, players explore different environments, interact with mission-related objects, complete objectives, and discover information about each piece of equipment. This includes why it was created, how it worked, the scientific instruments it carried, what it achieved, and what eventually happened to its mission. As players progress and complete their objectives, they collect stamps in their Space Passport, marking their discoveries and achievements. Once they have completed their journey, they can finally return to Earth.

Benefits for players: Our main goal is to help teenagers become familiar with space exploration equipment that they might otherwise never learn about. Many people recognize famous space missions but know very little about the actual machines that made their discoveries possible. Through our game, players get the opportunity to understand these machines, their purposes, and their contributions in a way that is interactive rather than simply reading paragraphs of information. They can enjoy an exciting adventure while learning real scientific and historical facts. The game also encourages curiosity by giving players opportunities to explore, ask questions, and discover information for themselves. We want them to finish the experience not only knowing more about NASA's equipment but also feeling interested enough to continue learning.

Intended impact: The game is primarily designed for teenagers aged 13–19, although anyone interested in space exploration, science, technology, and storytelling can enjoy it. We hope to make the stories of these machines more familiar to a younger generation and remind people that equipment left on other worlds should not be forgotten. Our intended impact goes beyond teaching players information during the game. We want them to become curious about the missions, search for additional information after playing, share what they have learned with their friends, and encourage others to experience the game. If a player finishes the game and decides to research another NASA mission simply because the experience made them curious, we will have achieved something meaningful. We want to turn a short gaming experience into a starting point for a much bigger interest in space exploration.

Creativity and originality: What makes The Last Signal different from traditional educational resources is the way scientific learning is built into the storyline. Instead of asking players to read about different machines, we give them a reason to discover them. The unexpected opening, where a mysterious green object in a refrigerator transports the player into space, creates a surprising beginning that immediately introduces the adventure. What starts as an ordinary moment at home becomes a mission to return to Earth. Learning about NASA equipment is no longer just an educational activity; it becomes an essential part of the player's journey. We also wanted to create an experience that keeps teenagers interested. Since our target audience may lose interest when information is presented in a traditional classroom format, we combined exploration, fictional guides, interactive objectives, discoveries, and the Space Passport to make learning feel like part of the adventure. The passport adds a sense of progress and achievement, encouraging players to keep exploring and complete their missions. Our creative direction was also influenced by elements of mystery and investigation, including inspiration from the game *Shift at Midnight*, while developing our own storyline, characters, and space exploration concept.

Tools and technologies: We used vibe coding and Google AI Studio to help bring our game prototype to life. This approach allowed us to turn our ideas, storyline, and planned gameplay into an interactive browser-based experience. Rather than beginning with a traditional educational presentation, we focused on developing a playable prototype in which the story and learning experience work together. Our development process involved translating the planned journey, environments, characters, and objectives into the game experience.

Team considerations and design decisions: During the design process, we considered our target audience, engagement, accessibility, scientific accuracy, and the overall flow of the gameplay. We chose teenagers aged 13–19 as our main audience and designed the experience to be engaging without making the scientific information too difficult to understand. We wanted players to remain curious throughout the journey, which is why we introduced a mystery at the beginning, fictional guides on each planet, mission objectives, and the Space Passport. We also chose a browser-based format so that players could access the experience using a computer without requiring specialized virtual reality equipment. Scientific accuracy was another important consideration. We based the educational information on NASA's official website and the NASA resources provided for the challenge, using real mission information to explain the equipment and its contributions. Finally, we considered the gameplay as a complete journey, making sure that the player has a clear reason to explore each environment, progress through the missions, and work towards the final objective of returning to Earth.

Ultimately, we wanted to create more than a game that teaches people the names of NASA's equipment. We wanted to create an experience that makes players care enough to discover the stories behind them. Through mystery, exploration, and interactive learning, The Last Signal turns forgotten space exploration equipment into the center of an adventure and reminds players that even when a mission ends, its discoveries deserve to be remembered.
